prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, and thereby changing the analysis of exporting, reallocation and the gains from trade

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework moved trade theory from representative industries to firms that differ in productivity and sort into exporting. This gave a new channel for the gains from trade through reallocation. It also tied theory directly to firm-level data, which reorganised empirical and quantitative trade work for two decades. It is a clear, single, checkable discovery with a well-defined originator in Melitz (2003). The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension on exporting versus FDI is a distinct and widely used second step. After the colleagues' arguments I still rank this first. Nothing I read changed my view of its scientific depth or maturity, which rests on more than twenty years of confirmation. The colleagues' points did sharpen my view of the attribution risk.
statement.case_against: Credit for the firm-heterogeneity idea is spread beyond the credited names. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and the Hopenhayn-style selection precursors, have parallel claims, and the ballot does not credit them. Helpman's strongest independent case may lie in B013 or in earlier new trade theory, so the pairing could be seen as stitching together a prize. Estimates of the welfare gains from selection depend on specification. Krugman's 2008 prize already covered the monopolistic-competition foundations of the field.

responses.point: Ranks B013 first. Grossman and Helpman form a clean, decades-long partnership. The protection-for-sale framework is a foundational, very mature model of political-economy constraints on trade policy, and their growth-and-trade work adds weight. Fredriksson also flags that Helpman's overlap with B041 complicates any Helpman award, and that empirical support for the model is mixed.
responses.response: I agree that the Grossman-Helpman pair is cleaner on attribution and at least as mature as Melitz-Helpman. The shared name is why I treat B013 as a rival configuration, not a complement. I weigh the protection-for-sale line below B041 because its empirical record is mixed, as Fredriksson concedes. B041 changed how trade is measured and estimated, and B013 mainly changed how policy formation is modelled. I do not think this is a decisive gap, so I list B013 as my first alternative. If the Committee wants a Helpman award, the live question is which achievement to credit him for, not whether he is a candidate.

responses.point: Ranks B041 seventh and proposes Melitz alone. He argues that Melitz is the clear originator and that a single name expresses the core discovery most cleanly, while noting that a prize might be shared with other trade theorists.
responses.response: I accept that Melitz is the origin of the core model, and a Melitz-only award is a coherent fallback. I still keep Helpman. The exports-versus-FDI extension and the trade-flow estimation work with Melitz and Yeaple turned the model into the operating framework of empirical trade. Leaving Helpman out would credit the idea and drop the step that made it usable at scale. I hold this as a judgement about attribution, not a settled fact. If colleagues think the extension is derivative, my fallback is Melitz alone, not a different configuration.

responses.point: Ranks B041 fourth and calls Melitz (2003) the central contribution. He stresses that credit is contested among Melitz, Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Helpman, that Redding's work is later, and that the size of the welfare gains from selection varies by specification.
responses.response: This is the strongest reservation against my first choice, and it lowers my confidence in the attribution even though it does not change my ranking. Because the ballot credits only Melitz, Helpman and Redding, the competing claim of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum cannot be honoured within this configuration. I think that argues for a narrow citation on selection and reallocation, not a broad one on all quantitative trade. I agree the welfare magnitudes are specification-dependent, but the prize-worthy result is the mechanism and its empirical consequences, not one gains-from-trade number. I rely on general knowledge here and have not independently verified the literature.

responses.point: Ranks B012 first. Kiyotaki-Moore is a very high-influence, mature macro-finance foundation, validated by 2008, and the core credit belongs cleanly to the pair. He sees the 2022 prize as a possible overlap but not a decisive one.
responses.response: I largely agree on merit and attribution, and B012 was my third choice. Boppart's point that the framework was borne out after 2008 is a fair one. I am less sure the 2022 overlap is a non-issue. Credit-constraint amplification sits close to the banks-and-crises theme, so I would give the Committee some caution on distinctiveness. I do not see a gap in quality between B012 and B041, only a modest difference in how much new ground each opens relative to prior prizes. I name B013 and B001 as alternatives because the protocol allows only two. B012 is a very close third for me.

uncertainties: How far the heterogeneous-firm credit extends beyond Melitz and Helpman, to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the ballot.
Whether the Committee prefers a Melitz-only award, a Melitz-Helpman award, or a Helpman award framed around B013.
Whether the 2008 prize for the monopolistic-competition foundations of trade leaves enough room for a second trade award.
How much weight the specification-dependent welfare estimates should carry against the strength of the mechanism.
My assessments rely on general knowledge, without independent source verification.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the B041 candidates (Melitz, Helpman, Redding) is apparent from the supplied profile. My profile shows frequent co-authorship with Per Krusell and co-authorship with Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, who are colleagues here. I am also an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. None of this bears on B041, but it could affect how I read their arguments. My research on social mobility is a disclosed interest relevant to B002, which is not part of my preferred configuration.
